title: Johnson Village Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Johnson Village wells have a median depth of 80 feet, with typical completed well costs of $11,200-$20,000.
intro_html:
Johnson Village sits in a mountain setting where most permitted wells draw from unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers. Records within 5 miles show a median well depth of 80 feet, a median reported yield of 12.0 gallons per minute, and a median static water level 40 feet below the surface.

Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for a particular lot. Bedrock fractures can change quickly from one parcel to the next. Before buying or building, review nearby well permits, ask for construction and pump records, and have a Colorado water professional confirm the proposed well location.

sections.heading: Johnson Village well depths and mountain bedrock
sections.html:
Johnson Village wells are generally shallow by mountain-well standards. The middle half of reported depths runs from 50 to 122 feet, and 60% are under 100 feet. Another 36% fall between 100 and 300 feet. The 90th-percentile depth is 198 feet, while the deepest recorded well reaches 700 feet.

For a drilling bid, the median is a starting point, not a promised refusal depth. The local ground is fractured granite and gneiss, so a driller may hit a productive fracture early or need to continue substantially deeper. A bid should explain the per-foot rate, casing and grout, testing, pump work, and what happens if the first hole does not produce enough water.

sections.heading: What Johnson Village wells produce
sections.html:
Reported well yield is usually workable for domestic use in this area. The median is 12.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. A large majority, 71%, report yields from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 26% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 3% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none are recorded under 1 gallon per minute.

These are reported pumping results, not a guarantee of household pressure or storage. Ask whether the test was a short yield test or a longer test, and check the well permit's allowed use. Most local permits are domestic or household wells. An exempt household-use well still has a 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels around Johnson Village
sections.html:
The median static water level is 40 feet below the ground surface, with the middle half between 21 and 75 feet. That helps with preliminary pump planning, but the actual water level depends on the lot, season, construction, and nearby pumping. A deeper static level also means more lift for the pump and can affect electrical and equipment choices.

The decade figures do not show a simple uninterrupted decline. Median depth to water was 28 feet in the 1970s, 25 in the 1980s, 30 in the 1990s, 31 in the 2000s, 51 in the 2010s, and 45 in the 2020s. The more recent readings are deeper than most earlier decades, but the records come from different wells and measurement locations, so they should not be treated as proof of a uniform water-table drop.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers near Johnson Village
sections.html:
The permit record shows long-term development around Johnson Village, with 20 permits in the 1950s, 44 in the 1960s, 311 in the 1970s, 210 in the 1980s, 522 in the 1990s, 473 in the 2000s, 360 in the 2010s, and 210 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2026. The records include 2,638 wells, although construction, depth, yield, and water-level information are not complete for every permit.

The most active listed drillers are Whitewater Systems, Inc. (Shake, Shawn), with 226 records; Twin Lakes Drilling Co. (Schaffer, James O), with 220; and Mccoy Drilling Inc (Dennison, Lynn A.), with 196. These records show local experience, but get current references and a written scope before hiring.

sections.heading: Johnson Village well drilling cost
sections.html:
Fractured mountain bedrock is the main cost driver here. The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole works out to about $5,200 to $8,000. A finished system, including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, is modeled at about $11,200 to $20,000.

That range can move when the hole must go deeper, access is difficult, casing or grout requirements change, or the pump must lift water from a deeper level. Treat the median-depth estimate as a planning figure rather than a fixed quote. Ask for separate prices for drilling, casing, grouting, testing, pump equipment, power, trenching, and any work needed to abandon an unsuccessful hole.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building near Johnson Village
sections.html:
Low yield is not the dominant pattern in the records, but fractured rock remains unpredictable and a nearby result does not guarantee the same result on your parcel. Review neighboring permits for depth, yield, static water level, construction, and intended use. Also verify water quality instead of assuming that clear water is safe.

Within about 10 miles, the mapped environmental record includes 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 353 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those maps do not by themselves prove contamination at a property, but they are reasons to order a well-water test and investigate mine or industrial history. Septic placement, replacement area, driveway access, drainage, and the building footprint must also be planned around the well and required separation areas.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot in Johnson Village
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the parcel and nearby properties. Confirm that the proposed use matches the permit, and check for any augmentation-plan issue if the property is in a basin where additional water use requires augmentation. An exempt household-use well is commonly used for domestic needs, but the permit terms still control.

For a new build, locate the well, septic system, access route, utilities, and house together before closing. Budget from the local $11,200-$20,000 finished-well model, then leave room for site-specific drilling and electrical work. Nearby Buena Vista, about 2 miles away, and Nathrop, about 5 miles away, provide useful local context, but the well record for the actual lot matters more than town averages.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Johnson Village?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Johnson Village is 80 feet. The middle half runs from 50 to 122 feet, 60% are under 100 feet, and the 90th percentile is 198 feet. The deepest recorded well is 700 feet, showing why fractured granite and gneiss can produce very different drilling outcomes on nearby parcels.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Johnson Village?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 80-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $5,200-$8,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at $11,200-$20,000. A deeper hole, difficult access, or additional casing and pump work can push the actual bid higher.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Johnson Village?
faq.a: The median reported yield is 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half from 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 71% yielding 5-15 gallons per minute and 26% yielding more than 15. No reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute, but fractured-bedrock results can vary between neighboring lots.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Johnson Village?
faq.a: Well-water safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Mapped sites within about 10 miles include 5 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 353 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well for relevant contaminants, review local mine and land-use history, and retest when conditions or ownership change.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Johnson Village?
faq.a: The recorded decade medians vary: 28 feet below surface in the 1970s, 25 in the 1980s, 30 in the 1990s, 31 in the 2000s, 51 in the 2010s, and 45 in the 2020s. Recent readings are deeper than most earlier ones, but different wells and locations mean this does not prove a uniform water-table decline.
